question: What are the core management responsibilities of an operating system?
correct: Managing processes, storage file systems, and hardware memory allocation
incorrect: Translating high-level source code into machine instructions before a program runs
Executing arithmetic and logic operations directly on data held inside the CPU
Storing the boot instructions permanently in read-only firmware on the motherboard
feedback: The operating system acts as the software manager between applications and hardware, overseeing processes, files, and memory.

question: In operating systems, what is a process?
correct: An instance of a running program managed and scheduled by the OS
incorrect: A program sitting on disk waiting to be launched by the user
A region of memory the OS reserves for a program's variables
A file in which a program keeps its settings between runs
feedback: A process is an active, executing program instance managed (started, scheduled, and isolated) by the operating system.

question: A laptop with a single CPU core appears to run a browser, a music player, and a text editor at the same moment. What is the operating system actually doing?
correct: Switching the core rapidly among the processes so each gets short turns
incorrect: Merging the three programs into one process that shares a single instruction stream
Giving each program its own block of RAM so the core can execute them literally at once
Keeping only one program in memory and loading the others from disk when clicked
feedback: One core can execute one instruction stream at a time, so the appearance of simultaneity comes from the scheduler slicing time finely enough that no human notices the gaps. Separate memory blocks keep the programs from corrupting each other, but memory is not what lets them share the CPU.

question: The part of the operating system that decides which process gets to use the CPU next is called the ___.
feedback: Deciding who runs next is a policy decision the OS must make thousands of times a second, and it is separate from deciding where a process's memory lives or which files it may open.

question: Why does one crashing app usually not take down the whole machine?
correct: The OS gives each process protected memory and mediates hardware
incorrect: Modern apps are written so carefully that their crashes stay contained
Each app runs on a separate processor core of its own
The hardware detects the crash and restarts that app
feedback: Programs ask the OS for what they need rather than commanding the hardware, and the OS decides. That mediation is the protection.

question: A site runs three server processes that take turns answering requests. One of them crashed days ago and nothing restarted it. What do visitors see?
correct: About one request in three fails, so the site seems to break at random
incorrect: Every request fails, since the three processes depend on one another
Nothing at all, since DNS stops sending visitors to a dead process
Every page loads, but each one takes about three times as long
feedback: The two survivors keep answering, so most requests work and the failures look random — to one visitor and not the next. The fault is not in the network at all: listing the machine's processes would show two where there should be three. A process that has crashed is simply gone, and unless something is watching for that, it stays gone.

question: What does the operating system's file system provide?
correct: Named files and folders, on top of storage that is really numbered blocks
incorrect: A protected region of memory for each program that is running
A schedule that decides which program uses the processor next
A directory that turns the names of websites into addresses
feedback: A disk stores numbered blocks of bytes and knows nothing of names. The file system is the layer that lets a program ask for "notes/todo.txt" and get the right blocks back — the third of the three things an OS manages, beside processes and memory.

question: What is the primary role of the Domain Name System (DNS) on the internet?
correct: Translating human-readable domain names into numeric IP addresses
incorrect: Delivering the packets of a message reliably and reassembling them in order
Assigning a numeric address to each device when it joins a local network
Carrying the request for a page and returning the response to the browser
feedback: DNS functions as the internet's phonebook, mapping domain names (like example.com) to numeric IP addresses.

question: Looking up the same big website twice can return different IP addresses. Why?
correct: Large sites run many machines behind one name, and DNS shares them
incorrect: Each visitor is permanently assigned their own private copy of the site
The address changes each time a page on the site is edited
DNS invents an address when the real one is unavailable
feedback: A busy site is not one machine: one name stands in front of many, and DNS hands out different addresses to spread visitors across them. It is also why a wrong DNS entry can make a site vanish for some visitors while everyone else sees nothing wrong.

question: A message of {{n}} bytes is sent in packets that each carry at most 1,000 bytes. How many packets does it take?
feedback_template: {{n}} bytes at 1,000 per packet rounds UP to {{expected}} packets: the last one is partly full, but the bytes in it still have to travel. Each packet is addressed and sent on its own, and they may arrive in any order.

question: What is the primary role of DNS caching in web networking?
correct: Storing recently looked-up domain IP mappings locally to reduce network query delays
incorrect: Storing copies of recently downloaded pages and images so they need not be fetched again
Storing each visitor's password so that a returning visitor is already logged in
Storing the results of recent database queries in server memory so repeats run faster
feedback: DNS caching saves recent domain-to-IP lookup results in local memory so subsequent requests avoid repeated DNS server lookups.

question: How does Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ensure reliable data delivery across the internet?
correct: By numbering packets, confirming receipt, and retransmitting lost packets
incorrect: By looking up the destination name and converting it into an address first
By encrypting each packet so nobody along the path can read or alter it
By sending each message as one large unit that routers deliver untouched
feedback: TCP provides reliable, ordered data stream delivery by breaking data into numbered packets and retransmitting missing ones.

question: A router along the path drops one packet in the middle of a TCP transfer. What happens next?
correct: The sender notices the missing acknowledgement and resends that packet
incorrect: The whole transfer restarts from its first packet
The receiver fills the gap by repeating the previous packet
The file arrives with a hole in it, which the browser reports as an error
feedback: TCP numbers packets and waits for acknowledgements, so a loss is detected and just that packet is resent. IP alone would simply have lost it.

question: These packets arrived out of order. Each carries its number and a piece of text. What does the program print?
code:
packets = [(3, "lo"), (1, "he"), (2, "l")]
packets.sort()
message = ""
for number, text in packets:
    message = message + text
print(message)
feedback: Sorting the pairs puts them in order of their numbers — 1, 2, 3 — and joining the texts in that order rebuilds the message. This is the job TCP does for you: packets are numbered when they are sent precisely so that they can be put back in order however they arrive.

question: A file is sent as {{n}} numbered packets. The receiver has acknowledged {{k}} of them. For how many packets is the sender still waiting on an acknowledgement?
feedback_template: {{n}} sent and {{k}} acknowledged leaves {{expected}} unconfirmed. TCP treats a packet as delivered only when its acknowledgement comes back; any of those {{expected}} that never gets one is sent again.

question: Arrange the four layers of the TCP/IP model, starting closest to the physical hardware.
feedback: The link layer moves bits between neighbouring machines; the internet layer routes packets between addresses; TCP, at the transport layer, makes the delivery reliable end to end; and the application layer is where HTTP and your program live.

question: Which of the following are layers in the four-layer TCP/IP network model? (Select all that apply)
incorrect: Session layer
Packet layer
feedback: The four TCP/IP layers are link, internet, transport and application.

question: The layer of the TCP/IP model that routes each packet across the world, hop by hop, toward its destination address is the ___ layer.
feedback: The Internet (IP) layer handles addressing and routing packets from network to network. Making that delivery reliable end to end is the transport layer's job.

question: Fetching a page takes three separate jobs in turn. First {{1}} turns the domain name into a numeric address. Then {{2}} routes the packets to that address, and the browser and server talk to each other in {{3}}.
feedback: Three different jobs, three different protocols: DNS resolves the name, IP routes the packets to the address it returned, and HTTP is the language the browser and server actually converse in once connected.

question: The standard protocol spoken between web browsers and web servers to request pages is ___.
feedback: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer foundation of web request/response communication.

question: NPC: What one click actually costs
intro: Tariq climbs to the ramparts. “You type a name and a page appears. Between those two moments is a short chain of separate errands. Most people cannot name even two.”

steps.say: You type example.com. Your machine has no idea where that is — names mean nothing to the network, which only routes to numbers. So errand one is DNS: ask the directory to turn the name into an IP address.

beats.say: You type example.com. Your machine has no idea where that is — names mean nothing to the network, which only routes to numbers.
So errand one is DNS: ask the directory to turn the name into an IP address.

check.prompt: The browser now has the IP address. What is the next errand?
check.answer: Open a connection to that address and send an HTTP request
wrong: Ask DNS again, this time for the page contents
Copy the server's files straight onto your disk
check.why: DNS only translates names into addresses. Fetching the page itself is a separate conversation, in HTTP, with the machine at that address.

steps.say: The server takes the request, runs its code, and sends back an HTTP response: a status code — 200 when all is well, 404 when there is nothing there — plus the HTML body. Your browser renders that. Each errand can fail on its own, and each fails in its own way.

beats.say: The server takes the request, runs its code, and sends back an HTTP response: a status code — 200 when all is well, 404 when there is nothing there — plus the HTML body.
Your browser renders that. Each errand can fail on its own, and each fails in its own way.

outro: “So when a page does not appear, the first question is: which errand broke?”

question: A browser reports "server not found" before any page loads. Typing the site's numeric IP address into the address bar instead works perfectly. Which errand failed?
correct: The DNS lookup: the name was never turned into an address
incorrect: The HTTP request: the server answered it with a 404 code
The rendering: the browser could not draw the HTML it got
The connection: the machine at that address is switched off
feedback: The machine is up and answering — the numeric address proves that. What failed is the errand before it: turning the name into that address. No connection was ever opened and no HTTP was ever spoken, so there is no status code to read.

question: Arrange the steps of fetching a web page, from typing the address to seeing the page.
items: Look up the domain name through DNS to get an IP address
Open a connection to that IP address
Send an HTTP request for the page
The server runs its code and returns an HTTP response
The browser renders the returned HTML
feedback: Names must become addresses before a connection can be opened, the request must go out before a response can come back, and only then is there any HTML to draw.

question: NPC: Reading the letter and its reply
intro: Tariq unfolds two slips of paper. “HTTP is plain text. If you can read these two slips, you can read any conversation on the web.”

steps.say: The request. Its first line says what is wanted: a method — GET means "give me" — then the path. Under it are headers: labelled notes about the request, one per line.

beats.code:
GET /tip/3 HTTP/1.1
Host: tips.example
Accept: text/html

beats.say: The request. Its first line says what is wanted: a method — GET means "give me" — then the path.
Under it are headers: labelled notes about the request, one per line.

steps.say: The response comes back in three parts.

beats.code:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found Content-Type: text/html

No such tip

beats.say: The response comes back in three parts.

check.prompt: Which line tells you how the request turned out?
check.answer: The first: the status line, with its code 404
wrong: The last line, with the heading in it
check.why: The status line carries the three-digit verdict. Headers describe the content, and the body IS the content.

steps.say: So: status line, then headers, a blank line, then the body. The first digit of the code is the gist — 2 worked, 3 look elsewhere, 4 your request was the problem, 5 the server was.

outro: “Another pair of slips. Read the first line of each before anything else.”

question:
Here is an HTTP exchange:

POST /orders HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example

HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: text/html

What went wrong?
correct: The server's own code failed while handling the request
incorrect: The request used POST, a method the server does not accept
The name shop.example could not be turned into an address
The browser was sent a page type that it could not display
feedback: The status line says 500, and a code starting with 5 means the server failed: the request arrived and was understood, and then something broke on the far side. A bad method would have been a 4xx — the client's mistake — and a DNS failure would have produced no response at all.

question: An HTTP response arrives in three parts. The {{1}} line carries the three-digit code such as 404, the {{2}} carry metadata such as Content-Type and Content-Length, and the {{3}} holds the HTML the browser actually renders.
feedback: Students often call the whole response "the page", but the parts have separate jobs: the code reports how the request went, the headers describe the content without being part of it, and only the body is the content itself.

question: Which of the following components are part of an HTTP request message? (Select all that apply)
incorrect: Status code, such as 200
Reason phrase, such as Not Found
feedback: A request carries a method, the path wanted, headers, and sometimes a body. The status code and its reason phrase belong to the response: they are the server's verdict on a request, so a request cannot contain them.

question: Which of the following are examples of HTTP request methods? (Select all that apply)
incorrect: SELECT
FETCH
feedback: GET, POST, PUT and DELETE are HTTP methods: the verb on the first line of a request. SELECT is SQL, and fetch is a name some libraries use for making a request — neither is an HTTP method.

question: Match each HTTP status code range to its general category.

pairs.definition: Success — the request was successfully received and processed
Redirection — further action must be taken to complete the request
Client Error — the request contains bad syntax or cannot be found
Server Error — the server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request

feedback: 2xx indicates success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client errors (like 404), and 5xx server failures (like 500).

question: The three-digit HTTP response status code that indicates a requested web page was not found is ___.
feedback: Status code 404 Not Found indicates that the server cannot locate the requested resource URI.

question: Which of the following HTTP status codes represent server-side errors? (Select all that apply)
incorrect: 200 OK
404 Not Found
feedback: 5xx status codes (like 500 and 503) indicate that the server encountered an error while attempting to fulfill a request.

question: A request is sent for a page that does not exist, and the program receives a 404 without crashing. What does this show?
correct: The server answered normally; the code reports it missing
incorrect: The server could not be reached, and 404 is how that is shown
The request completely failed to reach the server
The network dropped all the packets on the way back
feedback: A 404 is an answer. The request arrived, the server looked, and it replied — in an orderly response with a status line — that nothing lives at that path. Status codes are how HTTP reports failure as data rather than as silence or a crash.

question: A team moves its price list from /old-prices to /pricing and wants existing bookmarks to keep working. What should the server send when someone requests /old-prices?
correct: A 3xx redirect response naming the new location of the resource
incorrect: A 404, because the requested path no longer names a real page on the server
A 500, because the server can no longer complete a request for that path
A 200 with an empty body, letting the browser search for the moved page
feedback: The 3xx range exists exactly for resources that have moved: the browser is told where to go and follows automatically. A 404 would be honest but would break every bookmark, and a 500 would wrongly blame a server fault for a deliberate reorganisation.

question: What is the function of HTTP headers in a web conversation?
correct: Labelled notes about the message, such as its type and length
incorrect: The HTML or JSON content that the message exists to deliver
The three-digit code saying how the request turned out
The path naming which page or resource is being asked for
feedback: HTTP headers pass additional metadata (like content type, length, authorization credentials, and cookies) between client and server.

question: This program pulls apart one header line. What does it print?
code:
line = "Content-Type: text/html"
name, value = line.split(": ")
print(value.split("/")[1])
feedback: Splitting on ": " separates the header's name from its value, text/html. Splitting that value on "/" gives text and html, and index 1 is html. A header is just a labelled line of text, which is why two splits are enough to read one.

question: Loading a page takes one request for the HTML document itself, plus one request for each of its {{css}} stylesheets and each of its {{img}} images. How many HTTP requests does the browser send in total?
feedback_template: The HTML page is only the first request; every stylesheet and image referenced inside it costs another round trip, so 1 + {{css}} + {{img}} = {{expected}} requests.

question: A browser keeps {{parallel}} connections open at once and each connection can download only one file at a time. If the page needs {{files}} files, how many rounds of downloading are needed?
feedback_template: Each round moves at most {{parallel}} files, so {{files}} files need ceil({{files}} / {{parallel}}) = {{expected}} rounds; a partly full final round still counts as a round.

question: This function is meant to call 2xx codes "ok" and 4xx codes "error". What does the program print?
feedback: 404 is at least 200, so the first test passes and the function returns "ok" before the second test is ever tried. Ranges have to be checked from the top down — or with both ends, 200 <= code < 300 — or every error is reported as a success.

question: What is an Application Programming Interface (API) in the context of web applications?
correct: A web service designed to return structured data like JSON to code
incorrect: A styled web page built for a person to read in a browser window
The database engine that stores the records a website displays
The protocol that carries requests and responses between machines
feedback: A web API provides endpoints that applications call over HTTP to retrieve or update structured data (commonly JSON).

question: Which Python library is widely used to fetch web pages and call APIs from a program?
incorrect: flask
json
sqlite3
feedback: requests sends HTTP requests from a program. flask is for the other end — writing the server that answers them — and json and sqlite3 work with data you already have.

question: A response from the requests library is stored in the variable r. Write the Python expression that gives the numeric HTTP status code of that response.
feedback: The status code is an attribute already parsed from the response's status line, not a method you call, so no parentheses are needed. It is an int, which is why comparisons like == 200 work directly.

question: What method on a Python `requests` response object turns the body it received into a Python dictionary or list?
incorrect: .text
.content
.status_code
feedback: .json() reads the body as JSON and hands back the matching Python dictionary or list. .text is the same body as one long string, and .status_code is the three-digit verdict.

question: NPC: Walking into a JSON reply
intro: Tariq hands you a parcel within a parcel. “An API does not answer with a page. It answers with data — and data from an API is nearly always nested.”

steps.say: This is what .json() hands you: an ordinary Python dictionary. Some of its values are plain, one is another dictionary, and one is a list.

beats.say: This is what .json() hands you: an ordinary Python dictionary. Some of its values are plain, one is another dictionary, and one is a list.

steps.say: You walk in one step at a time. reply["now"] is the inner dictionary. To get the temperature out of THAT, you index again.

check.why: "temp" is not a key of the outer dictionary. It lives inside the dictionary stored under "now", so it takes two steps.

steps.say: A list is the same idea with a number: reply["next"][0] is 5. Read the brackets left to right, each one a step further in.

outro: “A different parcel. Count the steps before you write the brackets.”

question: This is the kind of dictionary an API reply becomes. What does the program print?
feedback: reply["plan"] is the inner dictionary, and ["name"] takes "pro" out of it. reply["tags"] is a list, and index 1 is its second item, "paid". Each pair of brackets is one step further into the reply.

question: An API reply has been stored as  data = {"city": "Oslo", "now": {"temp": 4, "sky": "snow"}}.  Write the expression that gives the temperature.
feedback: Two steps: data["now"] is the inner dictionary, and ["temp"] takes the temperature out of it. data["temp"] would fail with a KeyError, because the outer dictionary has no such key.

question: JSON arrives as text. This program turns it into Python data. What does it print?
code:
import json

text = '{"items": [{"id": 3}, {"id": 9}]}'
data = json.loads(text)
print(len(data["items"]), data["items"][1]["id"])
feedback: json.loads turns the text into a dictionary whose "items" key holds a list of two dictionaries. len counts the two, and data["items"][1]["id"] walks to the second one and takes its id. The braces and brackets in JSON become Python dictionaries and lists, one for one.

question: A program builds the address of an API endpoint. What does it print?
feedback: The f-string drops both values into place, giving https://api.example/weather/oslo. Split on "/", its last piece is oslo and the one before that is weather. Building a URL is string work you already know.

question: An API reply may or may not contain an "error" key. What does the program print?
feedback: .get() returns None for a key that is not there instead of stopping the program, which makes it the safe way to read a field an API only sometimes sends. reply["error"] would have raised a KeyError.

question: An API replies with  {"scores": [{{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}], "max": {{m}}}  and the program stores it in  reply.  What number is  reply["scores"][0] + reply["scores"][-1] ?
feedback_template: reply["scores"] is the list. Index 0 is its first item, {{a}}, and index -1 is its last, {{c}}, so the sum is {{expected}}. The {{b}} in the middle and the "max" value are never touched.

prompt: Fill in the blanks so this program asks a web API for Oslo's weather and prints the temperature from its JSON reply.
question:
import requests

r = requests.{{1}}("https://api.example/weather/oslo")
data = r.{{2}}()
print(data["temp"])
feedback: requests.get sends a GET request and hands back a response object. Its .json() method reads the body as JSON and returns ordinary Python data — here a dictionary, which is then indexed like any other.

question: Match each computing deployment model to its description.

pairs.definition: Renting raw virtual servers, storage, and networking hardware
Renting a managed platform to deploy code without managing servers
Using completed software applications hosted and managed by a vendor
Owning and maintaining physical server hardware in your own building

feedback: IaaS provides raw infrastructure, PaaS offers application deployment platforms, SaaS delivers end-user software, and on-premises uses self-owned hardware.

question: A student opens Google Colab in a browser and starts typing Python, with nothing installed. In cloud terms, what kind of service is that?
correct: SaaS: finished software, used through a browser
incorrect: IaaS: bare machines you put an operating system on
PaaS: a platform you upload your own web app to
On-premises: software running on your own computer
feedback: Colab is a finished application you simply use: that is software as a service. Underneath, it runs your code on a machine in someone else's data centre, which is why you have been a cloud customer all semester — but you never see or manage that machine.

question: Match each situation to the model it is an example of.

pairs.term: You rent a virtual server and install Linux on it yourself
You upload your Flask app and the service runs it for you
You log in to a web-based email program and use it
You keep a server in a closet at your own office

feedback: The question to ask is how much of the stack is yours to manage. On-premises: all of it, hardware included. IaaS: the machine is rented, the operating system up is yours. PaaS: only your code is yours. SaaS: nothing is — you are a user.

question: Which of these are reasons a company might choose SaaS over IaaS? (Select all that apply)
correct: Nobody on the team has to manage an operating system or servers
The software is ready to use immediately through a browser
incorrect: It gives the most control over exactly how the machines are configured
It is the model that keeps data on the company's own hardware
It lets the team install whichever operating system it prefers
feedback: SaaS trades control for convenience: you are a user, and nothing underneath is your problem. IaaS is the opposite trade — total control and total responsibility.

question: NPC: A route with a slot in it
intro: Tariq chalks three lines on the gatehouse wall. “You have been the one sending requests. Here is the other end: the code that answers them.”

steps.say: A route pairs a path with a function. The line starting with @ names the path; the function under it runs when a request for that path arrives, and whatever it returns is the response body.

beats.say: A route pairs a path with a function. The line starting with @ names the path.
The function under it runs when a request for that path arrives, and whatever it returns is the response body.

steps.say: A path can have a slot in it, written in angle brackets. Whatever the visitor puts in that part of the address is handed to the function as an argument: a URL parameter.

beats.say: A path can have a slot in it, written in angle brackets. Whatever the visitor puts in that part of the address is handed to the function as an argument: a URL parameter.

check.prompt: A request arrives for /tip/7. What happens?
check.answer: show_tip runs with tip_id equal to 7
wrong: status runs, because it is defined first
Nothing matches, since no path is exactly /tip/7
check.why: The slot matches the 7, and Flask passes it in as the argument named in the angle brackets.

steps.say: One function now answers for every tip there will ever be. That is the whole request/response cycle from the server's side: a request comes in, the matching function runs, its return value goes back.

outro: “A different route. Work out what the function is handed, then what it returns.”

incorrect: Hi, name!
Hi, <name>!
A 404 Not Found
feedback: The slot <name> matches Ada, so hello is called with name equal to "Ada" and returns "Hi, Ada!". The angle brackets are part of the pattern, never of the answer, and a slot matches any value — which is why this is not a 404.

question: Arrange these lines into a complete Flask app with one route.
feedback: Flask has to be imported before an app can be made from it, and the app has to exist before @app.route can attach anything to it. The decorator sits directly above the function it applies to, and the return belongs inside that function.

question: In a web application, an HTML file containing placeholders for dynamic server data is called a ___.
feedback: Templates are HTML files with placeholder tags where web servers insert dynamic data before serving the page.

question: The notebook says most web pages do not exist until you ask for them. What does that mean?
correct: A function builds the HTML on the spot from data and returns it
incorrect: Pages are stored as files but deleted after each visitor leaves
Pages are assembled inside the browser from data it already had
Pages exist just while a database query is still running
feedback: There is no file anywhere holding your social feed or your bank statement page. A page is just a string a server computed — and you already know how to compute strings.

question: Return True when an HTTP status code means success — any code from 200 to 299 — and False otherwise.
hint: A range has two ends. Python lets you write both in one comparison: `low <= x <= high`.
feedback: Checking only code >= 200 would call 404 a success. A range needs both ends, and the test table has a code just outside each one.

question: Return the kind of response a status code stands for: 'success' for 200 to 299, 'redirect' for 300 to 399, 'client error' for 400 to 499, and 'server error' for 500 to 599.
hint: Test the highest range first. Once a branch has returned, the next test only ever sees smaller codes.
feedback: The first digit is the gist of every HTTP response. Checking from the top down means each test needs only one end; checking from the bottom up, as the buggy trace earlier did, catches everything in the first branch.

question: Return the host name from a web address: the part after the two slashes and before the next slash, if there is one.
hint: Split the address on "/" and look at the pieces. The two slashes side by side leave an empty piece between them.
feedback: A URL is a string with a fixed shape: scheme, two slashes, host, then the path. Splitting on "/" gives the scheme, an empty string, and then the host at index 2 — the name DNS will be asked to look up.

question: An API reply is a dictionary with a 'days' list; each day is a dictionary with a 'high' and a 'low' temperature. Return the highest high in the forecast, or None when the list of days is empty.
hint: Loop over `reply['days']`; each item is itself a dictionary. Start `best` at None rather than at 0.
feedback: Real API replies are dictionaries holding lists holding dictionaries, and reading one is a loop plus two steps of indexing. Starting best at None instead of 0 is what gets the all-below-zero forecast right.

question: A file was sent as packets numbered 1 to total. Given the list of packet numbers that arrived (in any order), return a list of the numbers that are missing, smallest first.
hint: Walk the numbers from 1 to total with `range(1, total + 1)` and keep the ones that are `not in` the list.
feedback: This is the bookkeeping TCP does: because every packet is numbered, the receiver can say exactly which ones never arrived, and only those are sent again. range(1, total + 1) is needed because range stops one short of its end.

question: The part of a web address after the ? is a query string such as  city=oslo&units=c  — pairs joined by &, each a name and a value joined by =. Return it as a dictionary. An empty string gives an empty dictionary.
hint: Split on "&" to get the pairs, then split each pair on "=". Deal with the empty string before the loop.
feedback: Two splits and a dictionary: the same moves that read a header line. The values stay strings — "2", not 2 — because everything in a URL is text until a program decides otherwise.
